text: Something most people with focus issues never consider is how they are breathing. When you breathe through your mouth or overbreathe (which most people do without realizing it), you blow off too much CO2. Low CO2 causes blood vessels to constrict, including the ones feeding your prefrontal cortex. The Bohr Effect shows that hemoglobin holds onto oxygen more tightly when CO2 is low, so even with full lungs your brain gets less oxygen delivery. A Stanford experiment found that just ten days of forced mouthbreathing increased blood pressure by 13 points and destroyed sleep quality. Now imagine years of habitual mouthbreathing and what that does to sustained attention. I work with people on breath retraining and the ones who switch to nasal breathing and reduce their breathing volume consistently report better focus within weeks. Not because breathing is a magic fix but because their brain is finally getting proper blood flow and oxygen delivery. Normal breathing volume at rest is 4 to 6 liters per minute. Most stressed or anxious people breathe 10 to 15 liters. That gap is where a lot of concentration problems live.
